papers.title_in_file: The Race to Quantum Advantage Depends on Benchmarking
papers.version_note: The text is dated FEBRUARY 23, 2022 in its byline and carries a 2023 BCG copyright line. The text layer holds no content for Exhibits 1 to 5 (cited in the body as 'See Exhibit N'); only the body text, author list and boilerplate were available. The last two page breaks hold no text.
papers.what_it_is: A BCG consultancy article arguing that system and application benchmarks can accelerate quantum computing investment and adoption, with no new experiments or proofs.

assertions.value: The authors state that quantum computing technology attracted almost twice as much capital in 2020 and 2021 ($2.15 billion) as it had over the previous 10 years combined ($1.16 billion).
assertions.anchor: Opening paragraph, p.1 (Exhibit 1 not in text layer)
quotes: The technology attracted almost twice as much capital in 2020 and 2021 ($2.15 billion) than it had over the previous 10 years combined ($1.16 billion).
assertions.certainty_reason: A figure stated without a source in the text; the supporting exhibit is not in the text layer.

assertions.value: The authors state that hardware still attracts the most money, and that software investments jumped nearly 80% in 2020 and 2021 compared with the previous decade.
assertions.anchor: Opening paragraph, p.1 (Exhibit 1 not in text layer)
quotes: While hardware still attracts the most money, software investments jumped nearly 80% in 2020 and 2021 compared with the previous decade.
assertions.certainty_reason: A figure stated without a source in the text.

assertions.value: The authors report a Gartner prediction that 20% of organizations will be budgeting for quantum computing projects by 2023.
quotes: Gartner predicts that 20% of organizations will be budgeting for quantum computing projects by 2023.
assertions.certainty_reason: A forecast the paper attributes to another party and does not source further.

assertions.value: The authors anticipate that an additional $10 billion must still be invested in developing hardware to reach broad quantum advantage, and that end users will need to budget for quantum computing at twice the rate that they are today.
quotes: To reach broad quantum advantage, we anticipate that an additional $10 billion must still be invested in developing hardware, and that end users will need to budget for quantum computing at twice the rate that they are today.
assertions.certainty_reason: An authors' forecast with no method or data given in the text.
assertions.reader_inference: The text gives no derivation for the $10 billion figure.

assertions.value: The authors state that investors and end users have two needs: a business need (acquiring the knowledge to invest in or partner with individual providers confidently) and a technological need (assessing the maturity of providers' technologies and which hardware platform suits each of many potential applications).
quotes: investors and end users have two big needs. One is business-related: How do they acquire the knowledge required to confidently invest in, or partner with, individual providers?
What’s the best way to assess the maturity of individual providers’ technologies, and which hardware platform is best suited for each of many different potential applications?
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own framing of the problem it addresses, p.2.

assertions.value: The authors state that performance benchmarking means assessing the absolute and relative capabilities of different platforms or systems, and that benchmarks for quantum computing should be useful (they tell users what they need to know), scalable (they can expand and adapt to evolving technologies) and comprehensive (they cover all the relevant attributes).
quotes: Performance benchmarking—assessing the absolute and relative capabilities of different platforms or systems—has proved useful in assessing other deep technologies.

The key is designing benchmarks that are useful (they tell users what they need to know), scalable (they can expand and adapt to evolving technologies), and comprehensive (they cover all the relevant attributes)
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines performance benchmarking and its three design properties in its own words, p.3.

assertions.value: The authors state that benchmarks, by providing an objective measure of performance, can stimulate investment, promote healthy competition and deepen collaboration.
assertions.anchor: Section 'The Power and Complexity of Benchmarking', p.3
quotes: By providing an objective measure of performance, benchmarks can stimulate investment, promote healthy competition, and deepen collaboration.
assertions.certainty_reason: An authors' claim supported only by the genomics and MLPerf examples in the same article.

assertions.value: The authors state that sequencing the human genome took more than 10 years and about $300 million, that as recently as 2008 it cost a $1 million to do so for a single individual, and that the price has since dropped to about $1,000.
assertions.anchor: Section 'The Power and Complexity of Benchmarking', pp.3-4
quotes: it took more than 10 years and about $300 million to completely sequence the human genome.
As recently as 2008, it cost a $1 million to perform the process for a single individual.
the price of sequencing a complete human genome has dropped to about $1,000.
assertions.certainty_reason: Figures stated as background without sources in the text.

assertions.value: The authors state that the National Institute of Standards and Technology worked with the Genome in a Bottle Consortium to create a reference genome used to verify the accuracy of new sequencing technologies, and that other organizations later joined to create additional benchmarks, propelling development of next-generation sequencing platforms.
assertions.anchor: Section 'The Power and Complexity of Benchmarking', pp.3-4
quotes: the National Institute of Standards and Technology worked with a group of researchers, known as the Genome in a Bottle Consortium, to create a “reference
genome” that could be used to verify the accuracy of new technologies.
have since joined in the effort to create additional benchmarks, propelling development of next-generation sequencing platforms.
assertions.certainty_reason: A historical account of other work, not sourced in the text.
assertions.reader_inference: The causal link between the benchmarks and the price drop is the authors' framing; the text gives no evidence separating it from other causes.

assertions.value: The authors state that in machine learning the application-centric MLPerf benchmark suite has become the de facto performance standard, measuring the performance of graphics processing units on specific tasks such as image classification on a medical data set or speech recognition.
assertions.anchor: Section 'The Power and Complexity of Benchmarking', p.4
quotes: In machine learning, the application-centric MLPerf benchmark suite has become the de facto performance standard.
These benchmarks measure the performance of graphics processing units on specific tasks such as image classification on a medical data set or speech recognition.
assertions.certainty_reason: A statement about another field's benchmark, given without a source.

assertions.value: The authors state four reasons why benchmarking in quantum computing is more complicated than in other fields: the variety of systems built on fundamentally different technologies; different development rates and milestones, so that a static picture of today's market may not indicate future developments; very different application types (simulation versus optimization) that need different quantum configurations and forms of assessment; and the need to compare against classical computing, which advances through both hardware and algorithms.
assertions.anchor: Section 'The Power and Complexity of Benchmarking', p.4
quotes: Benchmarking in quantum computing is more complicated than in other fields for four key reasons.
The first is the sheer variety of quantum computing systems in development today.
Taking a static picture of today’s market and benchmarking performance against this state will not necessarily be indicative of future developments.
Third, much of the potential of quantum computing lies in very different types of applications—simulation versus optimization, for example
progress in classical computing continues not just through hardware advancements (which were steady and predictable thanks to Moore’s law) but also algorithmic advances (such as Google’s AlphaFold)
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the difficulties that frame its own argument, p.4.

assertions.value: The authors report that DARPA started a quantum benchmarking program 'to establish key quantum-computing metrics and then make those metrics testable', and they present this as a clear signal of the importance of benchmarks.
quotes: One clear signal of their importance is the move by the US Defense Department’s Advanced Projects Research Agency (DARPA) to start a quantum benchmarking program “to establish key quantum-computing metrics and then make those metrics testable”
assertions.certainty_reason: A quoted program statement relayed by the authors without a source citation in the text.

assertions.value: The authors state that early classical computing solved its benchmarking challenges with two types of benchmarks: systems benchmarks comparing base hardware performance with metrics such as instructions per second (IPS), and application benchmarks comparing performance on specific tasks, since peak IPS can differ significantly from speed on realistic workloads.
quotes: which were solved by developing two types of benchmarks.
by comparing base hardware performance with such metrics as instructions per second (IPS).
a computer’s peak speed in IPS can differ significantly from its speed handling realistic workloads
assertions.certainty_reason: A historical statement given without a source.

assertions.value: The authors state that system benchmarks measure fundamental characteristics of a quantum computer, and that IBM has a suite of system benchmarks covering scale (number of qubits), quality and speed.
assertions.anchor: Section 'Two Types of Benchmarks', p.7 (Exhibit 3 not in text layer)
quotes: System benchmarks measure fundamental characteristics of a quantum computer.
IBM has a suite of system benchmarks that cover scale (number of qubits), quality, and speed.
assertions.certainty_reason: A description of IBM's own benchmark suite; the authors thank IBM for assistance (p.13).

assertions.value: The authors define IBM's 'quantum volume' as a quality metric that gauges the maximum size square quantum circuit that a quantum processing unit (QPU) can reliably sample with a probability greater than 67%.
quotes: Quality is measured by what IBM calls “quantum volume,” a metric that that gauges the maximum size square quantum circuit that a quantum processing unit (QPU) can reliably sample with a probability greater than 67%.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own definition of the metric as it uses it, p.7.
assertions.reader_inference: IBM's published definition uses a heavy-output probability threshold of 2/3; the paper's 67% is a rounding and the paper does not name the sampled quantity.

assertions.value: The authors state that speed, introduced in late 2021, is measured in circuit layer operations per second (CLOPS), which corresponds to how fast a QPU can execute circuits.
quotes: Speed, introduced in late 2021, is measured in circuit layer operations per second (CLOPS), which corresponds to how fast a QPU can execute circuits.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own definition of the metric as it uses it, p.7.

assertions.value: The authors state that system benchmarks enable assessments of machine performance without regard to specific use cases, provide a clear record of progress, and are useful because many applications of quantum computing are sensitive to time to solution.
quotes: Such measures enable assessments of machine performance without regard to specific use cases and provide a clear record of progress.
They are useful since many applications of quantum computing are sensitive to time-to-solution.
assertions.certainty_reason: An authors' claim without supporting evidence in the text.

assertions.value: The authors report that for Shor's algorithm, which they say is commonly used to benchmark computational power because of its inherent complexity, the best estimate predicts an eight-hour run time for superconducting qubits, while trapped ion qubits, which have a lower CLOPs value, are estimated to take one year.
quotes: Shor’s algorithm, which is commonly used to benchmark computational power because of its inherent complexity, the best estimate predicts an eight-hour run time for superconducting qubits
trapped ion qubits, which have a lower CLOPs value, are estimated to take one year
assertions.certainty_reason: A cited estimate with no source, problem size or assumptions given in the text.
assertions.reader_inference: The text names no source, input size or error-correction assumptions for these run times, so the estimate cannot be checked from this paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that systems benchmarks are the most descriptive and most general benchmarks available and let vendors and code developers compare things like circuit depth, circuit width and gate density, but are often hard for end users to employ because they are technical and general, abstracting devices from end users' contexts.
quotes: Systems benchmarks are the most descriptive and the most general benchmarks available.
compare things like circuit depth, circuit width, and gate density.
they are often hard for end users to employ, not only because they tend to be technical, but because they are general.
assertions.certainty_reason: An authors' claim without supporting evidence in the text.

assertions.value: The authors state that application benchmarks show how well a quantum computer will perform at specific tasks, can help end users and investors evaluate the performance of an entire system on real-world use cases, and thus provide significant value beyond merely assessing quantum advantage.
quotes: This approach provides a view of how well a quantum computer will perform at specific tasks.

application benchmarks can help end users and investors evaluate the performance of an entire system and measure performance based on real-world use cases, thus providing significant value beyond merely assessing quantum advantage.
assertions.certainty_reason: An authors' claim without supporting evidence in the text.

assertions.value: The authors state that the quantum LINPACK benchmark measures the computer's ability to perform a key prerequisite computational task for linear algebra, while Q-score, a benchmark developed by Atos, measures performance on a full optimization problem by assessing the maximum number of variables a quantum processor can optimize.
quotes: the quantum LINPACK benchmark measures the computer’s ability to perform a key prerequisite computational task for linear algebra
Q-score, a benchmark developed by Atos, measures performance on a full optimization problem by assessing the maximum number of variables a quantum processor can optimize.
assertions.certainty_reason: A description of other parties' benchmarks, not sourced in the text.

assertions.value: The authors report that application benchmarks have shown that Advanced Quantum Testbed's quantum computer may outperform IonQ's machine when simulating quantum systems, while the reverse may be true for combinatorial optimization problems.
quotes: Application benchmarks have shown that Advanced Quantum Testbed’s quantum computer may outperform IonQ’s machine when trying to simulate quantum systems while the reverse may be true for combinatorial optimization problems.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result relayed without the benchmark, problem sizes, data or source; the wording is hedged with 'may'.
assertions.reader_inference: The text gives no benchmark name, circuit sizes or numbers for this comparison; it is an unsourced summary, probably of SupermarQ results, which the paper does not state.

assertions.value: The authors state that until quantum advantage is clearly established for practical use cases, classical high performance computers provide a standard for tracking progress, and that such comparisons help monitor the efficiency of the classical components of a quantum computer.
quotes: classical highperformance computers provide a standard to help users and investors track progress toward practical advantages in quantum computing.
these comparisons help monitor efficiency in the classical components of a quantum computer
assertions.certainty_reason: An authors' claim without supporting evidence in the text.

assertions.value: The authors state that quantum computations will eventually outpace classical yardsticks, so future benchmarks will need to track progress purely by comparing quantum devices against each other, and they quote DARPA program manager Joe Altepeter on measuring progress toward a useful quantum computer.
quotes: quantum computations will eventually outpace classical yardsticks.
Future benchmarks will need to be able to track progress purely by comparing quantum devices against each other.
we want to make sure we’re not quantifying progress toward that goal by measuring how high our planes can fly.
assertions.certainty_reason: An authors' prediction, with a relayed quotation.

assertions.value: The authors predict that application benchmarks will be a key focus in accelerating progress in the quantum computing market, and state that this requires manufacturers to permit their machines to be benchmarked for public review, with hardware providers adopting an ethos of openness.
quotes: We predict that application benchmarks will be a key focus in accelerating progress for the quantum computing market
this will require manufacturers to permit their machines to be benchmarked for public review.
Hardware providers will need to adopt an ethos of openness
assertions.certainty_reason: An authors' prediction and condition without supporting evidence in the text.

assertions.value: The authors state that, given the myriad potential applications for quantum computing, it is important to develop a suite of application benchmarks for a broad range of use cases, and that investors and end users need to evaluate machines against their specific goals.
quotes: Investors and end users need to evaluate quantum machines from the point of view of their specific goals.
it is important to develop a suite of application benchmarks for a broad range of use cases.
assertions.certainty_reason: An authors' claim without supporting evidence in the text.

assertions.value: The authors state that the US Quantum Economic Development Consortium (QED-C), established as a result of 2018's National Quantum Initiative Act, has developed a suite of application benchmarks targeted toward practical applications and based on executing common quantum algorithms or programs.
quotes: The US Quantum Economic Development Consortium (QED-C), which was established as a result of 2018’s National Quantum Initiative Act, has developed a suite of application benchmarks targeted toward practical applications and based on executing common quantum algorithms or programs.
assertions.certainty_reason: A description of another body's work, not sourced in the text.

assertions.value: The authors describe SupermarQ, a new application benchmark suite from the software startup Super.tech that applies classical benchmarking methodologies to quantum computing, with four design principles (scalability, meaningfulness and diversity, full-system evaluation, and adaptivity) and applications spanning finance, pharma, energy, chemistry and other sectors.
assertions.anchor: Section 'The Suite Spot', p.10 (Exhibit 4 not in text layer)
quotes: SupermarQ, a new suite of application benchmarks from the quantum software startup Super.tech that applies techniques from classical benchmarking methodologies to the quantum domain.
Four design principles— scalability, meaningfulness and diversity, full-system evaluation, and adaptivity—shape the selection and evaluation of applications
relevant to real-world use cases in finance, pharma, energy, chemistry, and other sectors.
assertions.certainty_reason: A description of Super.tech's own product; the authors thank Super.tech for assistance (p.13).
assertions.reader_inference: The paper reports no SupermarQ measurements; this is a description only.

assertions.value: The authors state that SupermarQ's algorithms cover most of today's use cases, that performance features such as critical depth or entanglement ratio help developers project how benchmarked systems would perform on any algorithm including custom ones, and that SupermarQ features an error correction benchmark as a proxy for practical readiness indicating how far a device has to go toward fault tolerance.
quotes: These algorithms cover most of today’s use cases.
performance features (such as critical depth or entanglement ratio) that help them project how each of the benchmarked systems
SupermarQ also features an error correction benchmark, a proxy for practical readiness that indicates how far a device has to go on the road to fault tolerance.
assertions.certainty_reason: A description of Super.tech's own product; the authors thank Super.tech for assistance (p.13).
assertions.reader_inference: No validation of the projection claim is given in this paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that investors and end users assessing quantum computing technologies and companies must consider critical decision factors, including the rigor and ambition of the provider's technical roadmap, the talent and reputation of the provider team, the financial terms of any deal (for investors), and the full benefits of a partnership such as talent sharing and onboarding programs (for end users).
assertions.anchor: Section 'The Critical Decision Factors', p.11 (Exhibit 5 not in text layer)
quotes: Each should assess the rigor and ambition of the provider’s technical roadmap and the talent and reputation of the provider team.

The financial terms of any deal are key for investors, of course, while scoping the full benefits of a partnership, including such issues as talent sharing and onboarding programs, are important concerns for end users.
assertions.certainty_reason: An authors' recommendation without supporting evidence in the text.

assertions.value: The authors state that investors can use systems benchmarks to gauge technology maturity and potential time to value, and application benchmarks to gauge the value creation potential of a technology, while end users can use application benchmarks to decide which hardware performs best on algorithms relevant to their workloads, such as the Variational Quantum Eigensolver for chemistry.
quotes: investors can use systems benchmarks to gauge tech maturity and potential time to value.
They can use application benchmarks to gauge the value creation potential of a given technology

End users will want to leverage application benchmarks to decide which hardware yields the best performance on algorithms relevant to their workloads (such as the Variational Quantum Eigensolver for chemistry).
assertions.certainty_reason: An authors' recommendation without supporting evidence in the text.

assertions.value: The authors recommend that investors and end users develop a comprehensive but measured approach that balances system and application benchmarks, leveraging work by organizations such as IBM, Super.tech and QED-C, and that investors track the benchmarks best suited to the solutions they fund to measure progress over time.
quotes: investors and end users should develop a comprehensive but measured approach that balances system and application benchmarks
leveraging the work of organizations such as IBM, Super.tech, QED-C, and others
investors can identify which benchmarks are best suited for solutions in which they want to put their money and track those metrics to measure progress over time.
assertions.certainty_reason: An authors' recommendation without supporting evidence in the text.

assertions.value: The authors conclude that the effective use of benchmarks will be a source of competitive advantage for investors and end users, that trustworthy benchmarks can accelerate progress across the ecosystem by stimulating investment in the right technologies, promoting healthy competition and deepening collaboration, and that effective benchmarking is critical to celebrating true advances and mitigating the impact of misleading information.
quotes: The effective use of benchmarks will be a source of competitive advantage for investors and end users.
Trustworthy benchmarks can also accelerate progress across the entire ecosystem by stimulating investment in the right technologies, promoting healthy competition and deepening collaboration
Effective benchmarking is critical to both celebrating true advances and mitigating the impact of misleading information
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' conclusion, argued by analogy in the text and not tested.

assertions.value: The authors state that breakthroughs in quantum computing have accelerated exponentially in recent years, but that these rapid advances are accompanied by both skepticism and misleading hype.
quotes: Breakthroughs in quantum computing have accelerated exponentially in recent years. But these rapid advances are accompanied by both skepticism and misleading hype.
assertions.certainty_reason: An authors' claim without supporting evidence in the text.
assertions.reader_inference: The word 'exponentially' is not backed by any measure in the text.

assertions.value: The authors state that they are grateful to IBM and Super.tech for their assistance with the article. The text reports no experiment, measurement or proof of its own.
quotes: The authors are grateful to IBM and Super.tech for their assistance with this article.
assertions.certainty_reason: The acknowledgment is stated on p.13; the absence of own results is the reader's check of the whole text.
assertions.reader_inference: IBM and Super.tech both appear in the article as benchmark providers (quantum volume, CLOPS, SupermarQ), so their descriptions carry a possible vendor bias.
